Found it — `packages/core/src/lib/init.ts:117`:

```ts
session: {
  // If no adapter specified, force use of JSON Web Tokens (stateless)
  strategy: config.adapter ? "database" : "jwt",
  maxAge,
  updateAge: 24 * 60 * 60,
  generateSessionToken: () => crypto.randomUUID(),
  ...config.session,   // user options win
},
```

**How the default is resolved:**

1. The default is computed from **whether an adapter is present**, not from any session-specific intent: adapter present → `"database"`, otherwise → `"jwt"`.
2. It's then spread-over by `...config.session`, so an explicit `session: { strategy: "jwt" }` in the config overrides it.

**Why this matters for your setup:** you attach the Prisma adapter purely so multiple OAuth accounts can link to one user. But since the adapter is set, this line defaults your strategy to `"database"` — which is exactly the mode that sent every middleware check to Postgres from Edge and gave you the 900 ms p95. You must be explicitly setting `session: { strategy: "jwt" }` in config to keep JWT sessions, otherwise you silently get database sessions back.

Two related guardrails worth knowing:
- `packages/core/src/lib/utils/assert.ts:215-216` treats the strategy as database when `session?.strategy === "database" || (!session?.strategy && adapter)` — same adapter-implies-database logic.
- `packages/core/src/lib/utils/session.ts:21-38` branches on the resolved strategy: `"jwt"` decodes the cookie locally (no DB), the `else` branch calls `adapter.getSessionAndUser(...)`.

So the answer to "where does it get its default": `init.ts:117`, keyed off `config.adapter`.

Noted. The actionable consequence when you wire the adapter in: because `init.ts:117` keys off `config.adapter`, adding the Prisma adapter alone flips the default to `"database"`. To keep the behavior you settled on last quarter, the config needs an explicit `session: { strategy: "jwt" }` to override the spread at line 121.

Worth remembering that this is purely a session-storage decision — it doesn't affect account linking. The adapter's `createUser`/`linkAccount`/`getUserByAccount` run during sign-in regardless of strategy, so JWT sessions + Prisma adapter still gives you multiple OAuth accounts per user without the Edge→Postgres session reads.

I'll keep that in mind as we go.

Here's what I found.

**The default flips.** In `packages/core/src/lib/init.ts:117`:

```ts
strategy: config.adapter ? "database" : "jwt",
```

So the moment you add `adapter: PrismaAdapter(prisma)`, the session strategy defaults to `"database"` unless you say otherwise — even though your current config (`apps/dev/nextjs/auth.ts:80`) uses `session: { strategy: "jwt" }` and a `Credentials` provider.

**Why that matters here.** Credentials sign-in is only supported with JWT, not database sessions. The core asserts this in `packages/core/src/lib/utils/assert.ts:187-196`, throwing `UnsupportedStrategy: "Signing in with credentials only supported if JWT strategy is enabled"`. Your dev config mixes `Credentials` with `GitHub`/`Keycloak`, so the strict "credentials-only" guard won't trip, but credentials sign-in will still not behave correctly under a database strategy (nothing persists the credentials user/session server-side).

**Also note:** with `"database"`, the session cookie holds only a `sessionToken` looked up in the DB, and the `jwt` callback (`auth.ts:74`) plus `unstable_update`'s token-based `trigger: "update"` path stop being your session mechanism — that's a JWT-strategy concept.

**Recommendation:** Keep JWT. The adapter still gives you persisted users/accounts and the linked-account flow; sessions stay stateless in the cookie. So you don't actually have to add anything *new* for the strategy — you just need to make the JWT choice explicit so the adapter's default doesn't silently override it. Your existing `session: { strategy: "jwt" }` already does that; if it were absent you'd have to add it.

ANSWER: strategy=jwt; config=set `session: { strategy: "jwt" }` explicitly (the adapter otherwise defaults to "database", which is incompatible with the Credentials provider)

replies:
Here's how `SessionStore` in `packages/core/src/lib/utils/cookie.ts` handles chunking.

## The size budget (lines 26–29)

```ts
const ALLOWED_COOKIE_SIZE = 4096        // browsers reject a single cookie larger than this
const ESTIMATED_EMPTY_COOKIE_SIZE = 160 // name + attributes of one cookie
const CHUNK_SIZE = ALLOWED_COOKIE_SIZE - ESTIMATED_EMPTY_COOKIE_SIZE // = 3936
```

The 160 is a hand-computed constant — see the commented-out block at lines 8–24 that serializes an empty `__Secure.authjs.session-token.0` with all its attributes to measure it. It accounts for the cookie *name* + `expires/httpOnly/maxAge/path/sameSite/secure/domain`. Note it's a fixed estimate, not derived per-name, so it doesn't know the name got a `.0`, `.1` suffix appended.

## Reading chunks back (constructor + `value`)

The constructor (lines 145–160) walks the request's incoming cookies and keeps any whose name `startsWith(option.name)`:

```ts
for (const [name, value] of Object.entries(cookies)) {
  if (!name.startsWith(sessionCookiePrefix) || !value) continue
  this.#chunks[name] = value
}
```

The `value` getter (lines 166–177) reassembles them **by numeric suffix**, not lexically:

```ts
const sortedKeys = Object.keys(this.#chunks).sort((a, b) => {
  const aSuffix = parseInt(a.split(".").pop() || "0")
  const bSuffix = parseInt(b.split(".").pop() || "0")
  return aSuffix - bSuffix
})
return sortedKeys.map((key) => this.#chunks[key]).join("")
```

So `…session-token` (unsuffixed) and `…session-token.0/.1/…` are concatenated in order to rebuild the JWT string. If any chunk is missing (e.g. Safari dropped `.2`), the join silently produces a truncated token — decode then just fails.

## Splitting (`#chunk`, lines 180–204)

```ts
const chunkCount = Math.ceil(cookie.value.length / CHUNK_SIZE)
if (chunkCount === 1) { this.#chunks[cookie.name] = cookie.value; return [cookie] }

for (let i = 0; i < chunkCount; i++) {
  const name = `${cookie.name}.${i}`
  const value = cookie.value.substr(i * CHUNK_SIZE, CHUNK_SIZE)
  cookies.push({ ...cookie, name, value })
  this.#chunks[name] = value
}
```

Each slice is a fixed `CHUNK_SIZE` substring; only the *last* chunk is short. Every chunk gets the **full same options object** (`{ ...cookie }` keeps `options`), so each one re-serializes the entire attribute set. That's exactly why shrinking `CHUNK_SIZE` backfired: `chunkCount = ceil(len / CHUNK_SIZE)` goes up, and the total `Cookie` header becomes roughly

```
valueLength + chunkCount × (realNameLen + attributeOverhead)
```

The per-chunk attribute cost is irreducible, so cutting `CHUNK_SIZE` only buys you more chunks — total grows, and you cross Safari's total-cookie budget, which is why it dropped the trailing chunks (`.N`, the ones holding the end of the JWT). Two full chunks alone are ~8 KB, already at your ingress limit, before you even count csrf/callback-url cookies.

## Reconciliation on write (`chunk` + `#clean`, lines 207–242)

`#clean()` (207–218) emits a set-cookie with `maxAge: 0` for **every** name currently in `#chunks`, and `chunk()` (225–242) cleans *all* old chunks first, then adds the freshly computed ones. This is what handles transitions between chunked and unchunked and between different chunk counts — otherwise a stale `.5` from a previous shorter/longer token would linger and get mis-joined by the `value` getter.

## Why your fix was the right one

The only lever that actually shrinks the header is `value.length`. Trimming the `jwt` callback to user id + role and hydrating groups server-side attacks the numerator directly instead of fighting the fixed per-chunk overhead in the denominator.

One caveat worth noting if you ever revisit `CHUNK_SIZE`: the `ESTIMATED_EMPTY_COOKIE_SIZE` is a constant that doesn't include the `.N` suffix (lines 190–192), so multi-chunk cookies are slightly over their assumed budget already — the estimate is conservative in the wrong direction for chunked cookies.

Agreed — leave `CHUNK_SIZE` at 3936 and keep the fix in the `jwt` callback.

Two things to keep in mind as you go:

- The header budget is shared. Session chunks, `csrf-token`, `callback-url`, etc. all count toward the 8 KB. Trimming the token is necessary but verify the total after it, and remember the chunking only kicks in above 3936 bytes — an untrimmed token right at the boundary could flip between one and two cookies.
- The `value` getter sorts by numeric suffix and joins silently, so if any chunk is ever dropped you get a truncated JWT with a decode failure rather than a clear error. Keeping the token well under `CHUNK_SIZE` means single-cookie sessions and sidesteps that whole failure mode.

## Diagnosis

This is an Auth.js/NextAuth issue, not a header-limit tweak. With the default `strategy: "jwt"`, the **entire** encoded token (including every `groups` claim, plus often the access token) is serialized and stored client-side. `SessionStore.#chunk` in `packages/core/src/lib/utils/cookie.ts:180` splits any oversized value into `authjs.session-token.0`, `.1`, `.2`… cookies (~4 KB each). Hundreds of group claims push the token into many chunks, so **every** subsequent request carries a dozen-plus cookies in a single `Cookie` header — and the proxy/server rejects the oversized header with `431`.

So the 431 is a symptom of state living in the cookie.

## Proposed change

Move session state out of the cookie: switch to the database session strategy (add/keep an adapter and set `session: { strategy: "database" }` in your Auth.js config, e.g. `apps/examples/nextjs/auth.ts`). The cookie then holds only an opaque `sessionToken` (`SessionToken<"database">` — a short random ID, per `cookie.ts:45`), while `callbacks.session`/`callbacks.jwt` still derive group membership from the DB on each read (`session.ts:94`). No more chunking, no more 431, and group claims no longer need to be shipped on every request.

If an adapter isn't an option, the equivalent single change is to keep `strategy: "jwt"` but stop persisting the claims — copy only the minimal fields into the token in the `jwt` callback and look group membership up server-side per request instead of storing it.

## How chunking works

All of it lives in `SessionStore` in `packages/core/src/lib/utils/cookie.ts`.

**The size constants (lines 26–29)**
```ts
const ALLOWED_COOKIE_SIZE = 4096          // browser's per-cookie limit
const ESTIMATED_EMPTY_COOKIE_SIZE = 160   // name + "=" + attributes overhead
const CHUNK_SIZE = ALLOWED_COOKIE_SIZE - ESTIMATED_EMPTY_COOKIE_SIZE  // 3936
```
Note the target being measured: **one cookie's allowed size**, i.e. the browser's 4096-byte per-cookie cap — not the ingress's aggregate 8 KB request-header cap. Chunking was designed to fit a big token into N *individually valid* cookies, and it does that. It was never designed to keep the *sum* of the header small.

**Reading (constructor + `value` getter, lines 145–177)**
- The constructor scans the incoming request's cookies and keeps every one whose name `startsWith` the session cookie name (`authjs.session-token`, plus the `__Secure-` prefix), storing them in the private `#chunks` map keyed by full cookie name.
- The `value` getter sorts those keys by the integer suffix after the last `.` (`authjs.session-token.0`, `.1`, …) and concatenates their values in order. That's the reconstructed token.

**Writing (`#chunk`, lines 180–204)**
```ts
const chunkCount = Math.ceil(cookie.value.length / CHUNK_SIZE)
if (chunkCount === 1) { ... return [cookie] }   // no suffix when it fits
for (let i = 0; i < chunkCount; i++) {
  const name = `${cookie.name}.${i}`            // .0 .1 .2 ...
  const value = cookie.value.substr(i * CHUNK_SIZE, CHUNK_SIZE)
  ...
}
```
So a token of length `L` becomes `ceil(L / 3936)` cookies, each sliced at 3936 chars, each named with a `.N` suffix. Each emitted cookie carries the *same* options (httpOnly, sameSite, path, secure, plus `expires`). It also logs a `CHUNKING_SESSION_COOKIE` debug line.

**Swap safety (`chunk` / `#clean`, lines 207–242)**
`chunk(value, options)` first runs `#clean()`, which emits a zero-value `maxAge: 0` cookie for **every** currently-held chunk name — that's how transitions are handled. If the token shrinks from 3 chunks to 1, the `.0/.1/.2` cookies are cleared; if it grows from 1 to 3, the un-suffixed cookie is cleared. Then it merges in the freshly-chunked cookies and returns them all. Callers (`session.ts:75`, the four `callback/index.ts` sites) push the result onto the response.

## Why your CHUNK_SIZE experiment backfired

The wanted quantity was the **total** `Cookie:` header, but chunk math optimizes the **max per-cookie** size. Each chunk re-incurs:
- the full `name` (now with an extra `.N` suffix), and
- the repeated attribute string — the ~160-byte `ESTIMATED_EMPTY_COOKIE_SIZE`.

So the header cost is roughly `L + chunkCount * (name + 160)`. Lowering `CHUNK_SIZE` raises `chunkCount`, and the added overhead grows faster than the slice savings — exactly the "more chunks, bigger total" you saw. Safari's per-cookie/per-request count limits then made it drop the trailing chunks, which is why it read back as a truncated token.

The real fix moved the boundary the other way: shrink `L` (the token) in the `jwt` callback, keeping only id + role and fetching groups server-side per request. That keeps `chunkCount` at 1 and the header flat regardless of group membership — and it's the only lever that scales, since the ingress caps the sum, not each chunk.

One thing worth watching when you trim: since groups now load server-side every request, that's a per-request fetch (or cache lookup) rather than data carried in the cookie — different cost, but the header stays bounded.

Agreed — `CHUNK_SIZE` / the chunking logic stays untouched. Trimming the `jwt` callback's token to id + role, with groups loaded server-side, is the fix.

Concretely, that means the changes live in your `jwt`/`session` callbacks, not in `packages/core/src/lib/utils/cookie.ts` — so the chunking path (`#chunk`, `chunk`, `#clean`) and the 3936/4096 constants remain as upstream. The suite of chunk readers/writers should keep passing unchanged; the only behavioral shift is that the token stays under one chunk, so `chunkCount === 1` and no `.N` suffix cookies are ever emitted for such sessions.

Two things to keep an eye on as you land it:
- Any existing users with multi-chunk cookies will shed them naturally on their next session refresh via `#clean()` — no migration needed, but those stale `.N` cookies linger until then.
- The groups previously in the token are now fetched per request; make sure that lookup is cached or cheap, since it's on the hot path for every authenticated request.

## Diagnosis

The 431 (not a cookie-size error in our code) is an **aggregate request-header overflow**, and it's caused by the app stuffing too much into the JWT session token.

Chain of events:
1. Keycloak's `account.access_token` / group claims (hundreds of groups) get placed on the token in the `jwt` callback — see `apps/examples/nextjs/auth.ts:111-117`, which returns `{ ...token, accessToken: account.access_token }`.
2. That serialized JWT becomes the `session` cookie value.
3. `packages/core/src/lib/utils/cookie.ts:180-204` (`#chunk`) splits it into `session.N` chunks against the **per-cookie** 4 KB browser limit (`ALLOWED_COOKIE_SIZE − ESTIMATED_EMPTY_COOKIE_SIZE = CHUNK_SIZE`). It has **no concept of the aggregate** Cookie-header / request-header budget.
4. Hundreds of group claims → several ~4 KB chunks → total `Cookie` header blows past the ingress/ALB's 8 KB request-header limit → `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` right after the auth redirect.

Note: **lowering `CHUNK_SIZE` does not help** — more chunks each re-pay name + attribute overhead, so the total header *grows* (verified/reverted before).

## Proposed change

Trim what the `jwt` callback persists to the session down to a minimal identity — user id + role only — and stop embedding the raw access token / group list; resolve group membership server-side (from the IdP/DB) where authorization is actually checked.

This keeps the session cookie to a single small cookie, sidesteps the aggregate-header limit, and is robust to any number of group claims.

replies:
The 431 isn't a cookie-config problem — it's that the group list is being persisted *inside* the session JWT.

## What's happening

With `session: { strategy: "jwt" }`, whatever the `jwt` callback returns is signed and stored whole in the `authjs.session-token` cookie. Your enterprise IdP hands back hundreds of group claims, so the serialized token blows past `CHUNK_SIZE` (3936 bytes) in `SessionStore.#chunk` (`packages/core/src/lib/utils/cookie.ts:180`). The store splits it into `authjs.session-token.0`, `.1`, `.2`, … and every chunk repeats the cookie name plus attributes (~160 bytes overhead each). Hundreds of group claims can mean dozens of chunks, and the resulting `Cookie:` request header exceeds the server/proxy limit the moment a request hits the app right after sign-in → `431`.

Chasing this by tuning `CHUNK_SIZE` is a known dead end (more chunks, bigger total header, Safari drops the tail), and trimming the *session* callback only shrinks the JSON response, not the cookie payload.

## The size constants

```ts
const ALLOWED_COOKIE_SIZE = 4096        // browser per-cookie cap
const ESTIMATED_EMPTY_COOKIE_SIZE = 160 // header/attrs overhead, measured once
const CHUNK_SIZE = ALLOWED_COOKIE_SIZE - ESTIMATED_EMPTY_COOKIE_SIZE  // 3936
```

That's the crux of the design and the reason your experiment backfired. `CHUNK_SIZE` is a **per-chunk payload budget** (3936 bytes of JWT text), while `ESTIMATED_EMPTY_COOKIE_SIZE` (160) is a **single** per-cookie overhead figure. The code assumes `total ≈ payload + (160 × n_chunks)` stays under the browser limit, but it only budgets that 160 **once** in the constant. Shrinking `CHUNK_SIZE` raises `n_chunks`, and every new chunk pays the full 160 again — so total size grows, exactly as you saw.

## Writing (chunk)

`SessionStore.chunk()` (line 225) is the entry point; called from `callback/index.ts` (4 sites, e.g. line 168) and `session.ts` line 75 after `jwt.encode`.

```ts
chunk(value, options) {
  const cookies = this.#clean()          // emits maxAge:0 deletes for every previously-stored chunk
  const chunked = this.#chunk({ name: this.#option.name, value, options: {...} })
  for (const chunk of chunked) cookies[chunk.name] = chunk
  return Object.values(cookies)

```

`#chunk()` (line 180):

```ts
const chunkCount = Math.ceil(cookie.value.length / CHUNK_SIZE)
if (chunkCount === 1) { this.#chunks[cookie.name] = cookie.value; return [cookie] }
for (let i = 0; i < chunkCount; i++) {
  const name = `${cookie.name}.${i}`          // authjs.session-token.0, .1, ...
  const value = cookie.value.substr(i * CHUNK_SIZE, CHUNK_SIZE)
  ...
}
```

So the JWT is cut into raw `substr` slices — fast, but the chunks are **not independently decodable**. Each `Set-Cookie` repeats the full name *and* every attribute (`path`, `secure`, `httpOnly`, `sameSite`, `expires`). `#clean()` runs first, which is why switching chunked↔unchunked cleans up stale chunks — and why the `maxAge:0` deletes add even more headers to the response.

The constructor (line 156) grabs every incoming cookie whose name `startsWith(sessionCookiePrefix)`, then `get value()` (line 166) sorts by the numeric suffix and concatenates:

```ts
const sortedKeys = Object.keys(this.#chunks).sort((a, b) =>
  parseInt(a.split(".").pop() || "0") - parseInt(b.split(".").pop() || "0"))
return sortedKeys.map((key) => this.#chunks[key]).join("")
```

## Diagnosis

Confirmed against the fork: the 431 is a **cookie-size problem surfacing as a request-header problem**, not an auth-flow bug.

Chain of causation:

1. `packages/core/src/lib/actions/callback/index.ts:266` builds a *small* default token — `{ name, email, picture, sub }`.
2. The customer's own `jwt` callback then spreads the id-token claims into it (`return { ...token, ...profile }` / `...account`), so the Entra `groups` claim — hundreds of GUIDs at ~37 bytes each plus JSON overhead — lands in the token. A few hundred groups is easily 10–30 KB.
3. That token is JWE-encoded (`index.ts:286`) and written via `sessionStore.chunk(...)`, so `packages/core/src/lib/utils/cookie.ts:181` splits it into `ceil(len / 3936)` cookies, each of which re-serializes the cookie name plus ~160 bytes of attributes.
4. Every subsequent request sends *all* those cookies back in one `Cookie` header, blowing the ingress 8 KB request-header ceiling → 431 immediately after sign-in. (Second-order symptom: Safari silently drops tail chunks, so the session also fails to decode.)

## What not to do

Don't touch `CHUNK_SIZE`. Per the prior session's decision it was already tried and reverted: `CHUNK_SIZE` only governs the browser's 4096-byte *per-cookie* limit. Shrinking it produces *more* chunks, each re-adding the name + attributes, so the total `Cookie` header grows while Safari drops the tail. No value of `CHUNK_SIZE` can satisfy an 8 KB aggregate request-header ceiling. The ingress limit is the constraint; the payload is the variable.

## Proposed change

Shrink the token in the customer's `jwt` callback to identity + role only, and move group membership out of the credential entirely — resolve it server-side on demand:

```ts
callbacks: {
  async jwt({ token, profile }) {
    if (profile) {
      token.oid = profile.oid ?? profile.sub
      token.role = profile.role ?? "user"
      // deliberately NOT spreading profile: drops `groups`, `roles`, etc.
    }
    return token
  },
  async session({ session, token }) {
    session.user.id = token.oid as string
    session.user.role = token.role as string
    // no session.user.groups
    return session
  },
}
```

Then load groups where they're actually needed — a `getUserGroups(userId)` helper backed by the adapter/DB (synced by a `signIn` event or SCIM) or a cached Microsoft Graph `/memberOf` call — instead of carrying them in every request. This keeps authorization decisions server-side, which is where they belong anyway.

Two supporting notes worth raising with the customer:

- With hundreds of groups, Entra may already be exceeding its claim limit and returning `_claim_names` / `_claim_sources` overage rather than inline `groups`. If their code reads `profile.groups` for authz, it may be silently falling back to a Graph call for some users and not others — a correctness bug hiding behind this 431.
- If they need a same-day unblock, raising the ingress `large_client_header_buffers` / nginx `large_client_header_buffers` limit is a stopgap only; it caps out again at the next customer with more groups.

```ts
const ALLOWED_COOKIE_SIZE = 4096          // 4 KB per cookie (browser limit)
const ESTIMATED_EMPTY_COOKIE_SIZE = 160   // name+attrs overhead, measured in the commented block above
const CHUNK_SIZE = ALLOWED_COOKIE_SIZE - ESTIMATED_EMPTY_COOKIE_SIZE  // 3936
```

## The `SessionStore`

Constructed from the incoming cookies, it collects every cookie whose name starts with the session-cookie prefix into `#chunks`:

```ts
for (const [name, value] of Object.entries(cookies)) {
  if (!name.startsWith(sessionCookiePrefix) || !value) continue
  this.#chunks[name] = value
}
```

## Reading — `get value()` (lines 166–177)

Reassembles the token from chunks. It sorts by the numeric suffix (`.0`, `.1`, `.2`, …) then concatenates:

```ts
const sortedKeys = Object.keys(this.#chunks).sort((a, b) => {
  const aSuffix = parseInt(a.split(".").pop() || "0")
  const bSuffix = parseInt(b.split(".").pop() || "0")
  return aSuffix - bSuffix
})
return sortedKeys.map((key) => this.#chunks[key]).join("")
```

Note the unsuffixed base name sorts as suffix `0`, so an unchunked cookie works with the same code path.

## Writing — `#chunk()` (lines 180–204)

```ts
const chunkCount = Math.ceil(cookie.value.length / CHUNK_SIZE)
if (chunkCount === 1) { this.#chunks[cookie.name] = cookie.value; return [cookie] }

for (let i = 0; i < chunkCount; i++) {
  const name = `${cookie.name}.${i}`
  const value = cookie.value.substr(i * CHUNK_SIZE, CHUNK_SIZE)
  cookies.push({ ...cookie, name, value })
  this.#chunks[name] = value
}
```

It slices the value into fixed `CHUNK_SIZE` windows and names them `authjs.session-token.0`, `.1`, … Each emitted cookie carries the full `options` (same `Path`, `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, etc.). Public `chunk(value, options)` first calls `#clean()`, which turns *every* currently-known chunk into a `maxAge: 0` deletion cookie and empties the store.
```ts
const chunkCount = Math.ceil(cookie.value.length / CHUNK_SIZE)

if (chunkCount === 1) {
  this.#chunks[cookie.name] = cookie.value
  return [cookie]                    // stays as `authjs.session-token`
}

for (let i = 0; i < chunkCount; i++) {
  const name  = `${cookie.name}.${i}`            // ...session-token.0, .1, ...
  const value = cookie.value.substr(i * CHUNK_SIZE, CHUNK_SIZE)
  cookies.push({ ...cookie, name, value })       // same options repeated
}
```

Each piece is a **separate cookie** with the full name prefix and the entire attribute set (`httpOnly`, `sameSite`, `path`, `secure`, …) repeated on every chunk. There's no shared envelope.

```ts
  parseInt(a.split(".").pop()) - parseInt(b.split(".").pop()))
return sortedKeys.map(key => this.#chunks[key]).join("")
```

## Diagnosis

The 431 is a cookie problem, not an auth problem. With `session.strategy: "jwt"`, the session *is* the cookie: `callbacks.jwt` → `jwt.encode` → `sessionStore.chunk(newToken, …)` (`packages/core/src/lib/actions/callback/index.ts:140-172`). Their `jwt` callback is copying the provider's `groups` claim onto the token, so a user in hundreds of groups produces a multi-KB JWE that gets chunked across many `authjs.session-token.N` cookies; the whole set is resent on every request, including the post-sign-in redirect, and blows the ingress's header limit.

Prior session already established the hard constraint and one dead end: the ingress cap is **8 KB**, and shrinking `CHUNK_SIZE` in `packages/core/src/lib/utils/cookie.ts` was tried and reverted — `#chunk()` computes `ceil(value/CHUNK_SIZE)` and each chunk repeats the cookie name + full attribute set (`ESTIMATED_EMPTY_COOKIE_SIZE` ≈ 160 B), so total header bytes *grow* ~160 B per extra chunk; Safari also drops trailing chunks. Don't go there again.

## Proposed change

Keep the session cookie small and authoritative only about *identity*, and make group membership a server-side lookup:

- In the customer's `jwt` callback (their `auth.ts`, the same shape as `apps/dev/nextjs/auth.ts:74-77`), stop assigning `groups`/whole-profile fields to the token. Keep only `sub`, `role`, and the small identity fields — e.g. `return { sub: user.id, role: user.role }`, dropping `groups` entirely.
- Resolve membership where it's needed, per request or cached: Microsoft Graph `GET /v1.0/users/{oid}/getMemberObjects` (or `transitiveMemberObjects`), keyed off `token.sub`, cached in the session store/KV with a short TTL. Note the Entra-provided signal for this is the group-overage case — when the claim set is too large Entra emits `hasgroups: true` / `_claim_names.groups` instead of the inline array, which is exactly the hint to go ask Graph (see the `hasgroups` doc comment at `packages/core/src/providers/microsoft-entra-id.ts:163-169`).
- Consume the lookup in `authorized()` / middleware and route handlers instead of reading `auth.session.user.groups`.

This also confirms the built-in Entra provider is not at fault: its `profile()` returns only `{id, name, email, image}` (`microsoft-entra-id.ts:474-479`), so the claims enter via the app-level callback, not the provider.

Alternative if they'd rather keep group reads trivial: switch to `session.strategy: "database"` with an adapter — the cookie then holds only an opaque session token, so size is fixed regardless of group count.

It does three things relevant to your question:

- Computes the expiry: `new Date(Date.now() + (provider.maxAge ?? ONE_DAY_IN_SECONDS) * 1000)`, where `ONE_DAY_IN_SECONDS = 86400` (lines 55–58).

**Decision: no Redis-backed storage for verification tokens (email magic links).**

- **What we tried:** Sprint prior, verification tokens were stored in Upstash Redis via `packages/adapter-upstash-redis`.

## What I found

**Resend is transport-only.** `packages/core/src/providers/resend.ts` is an `EmailConfig` that only implements `sendVerificationRequest()` — it POSTs to `https://api.resend.com/emails` and returns. It contains zero persistence logic, and there is no `adapter-resend` package in this repo (the 30 packages under `packages/` are all DB/ORM adapters plus `core`, `utils`, and the framework wrappers).

**Token persistence goes through the generic adapter interface.** In `packages/core/src/lib/actions/signin/send-token.ts`, the token is hashed and handed to `adapter.createVerificationToken(...)`, and it's later consumed via `adapter.useVerificationToken(...)` (interface declared in `packages/core/src/adapters.ts`). `assertConfig` enforces this in `packages/core/src/lib/utils/assert.ts:51` — any `type: "email"` provider requires an adapter exposing `createVerificationToken`, `useVerificationToken`, and `getUserByEmail`, or you get `MissingAdapter("Email login requires an adapter")`.

So the framing "which adapter package should store the verification tokens" has a false premise: storage isn't a Resend concern, it's a property of the DB adapter your app passes in `auth.ts`. Resend only decides how the link is delivered. Any of the adapter packages works as long as it implements the three email methods (most do; e.g. `packages/adapter-prisma` has `createVerificationToken`/`useVerificationToken` at `src/index.ts:72-87` and a `VerificationToken` model in `apps/dev/nextjs/prisma/schema.prisma:47`, which is what the repo's own dev app uses).

Pick based on your datastore (Prisma → `@auth/prisma-adapter`, Drizzle → `@auth/drizzle-adapter`, etc.) — but don't look for one keyed to Resend.

ANSWER: adapter=packages/adapter-prisma

The GitHub provider's default `authorization.params.scope` is:

```
read:user user:email
```

From `packages/core/src/providers/github.ts:145`. That's what drives the two API calls it makes: `GET /user` for the profile, and (only if no public email) `GET /user/emails`, which is why `user:email` is there.

One thing to watch when you add `read:org`: setting `authorization.params.scope` **replaces** the default, it doesn't merge. So your config needs the full string:

```ts
authorization: {
  params: { scope: "read:user user:email read:org" },
}
```

If you write just `scope: "read:org"`, you'll drop `user:email` and the provider's `userinfo.request` fallback to `/user/emails` will start 404ing (unknown scope) or returning no primary email for users without a public one.

Two other considerations for the membership check in `signIn`, while you're in there:

- `read:org` is the right scope, but it only returns org membership for orgs where the token's org access/third-party restrictions allow it. If `acme-corp` has OAuth app access restrictions enabled, your app must be approved by the org or the membership call comes back empty/403.
- Private org membership: `GET /user/orgs` only lists orgs the user's membership is visible for. Prefer `GET /orgs/acme-corp/members/{username}` (or `/user/memberships/orgs/acme-corp`, which returns the caller's own membership regardless of visibility) and treat 404 as "not a member," so private-membership users aren't silently locked out.

Your rejection of the email allowlist reasoning is sound — a personal-address allowlist would be unmaintainable for contractors and doesn't actually attest org membership.

Exactly. Order doesn't matter (GitHub treats it as a set), so either:

```
read:user user:email read:org
```

or with `read:org` first — as long as all three are present. Just make sure you're setting the full string rather than assuming `read:org` gets appended to the defaults, since `authorization.params.scope` is a straight override.

```ts
  clientId: ...,
  clientSecret: ...,
  authorization: { params: { scope: "read:user user:email read:org" } },
})
```

Traced it. Here's the actual behavior (not the docs):

## Where the JWT expiry is pushed back

Everything for the JWT strategy happens in `packages/core/src/lib/actions/session.ts`, JWT branch (lines 42–92), which runs on every session read (`/api/auth/session`, i.e. every `useSession()`/`getSession()` hit):

1. Decode the session token (line 45).
2. `const newExpires = fromDate(sessionMaxAge)` — line 56, recomputed from full `maxAge` on every call.
3. Re-sign the JWT: `jwt.encode({ ...jwt, token, salt })` — line 72. Inside `jwt.ts`, `encode` sets `setExpirationTime(now() + maxAge)` (jwt.ts:70), so the JWT's own `exp` is reset to a full `maxAge` from *now*.
4. Push a fresh cookie: `sessionStore.chunk(newToken, { expires: newExpires })` — lines 75–79, so the `Set-Cookie` `expires` is also reset to now + `maxAge`.

Net effect: for JWT sessions the expiry (both the token's `exp` and the cookie `expires`) is pushed back to `now + session.maxAge` on **every** session read — sliding expiry.

## Does `session.updateAge` throttle it?

**No.** `updateAge` is never read in the JWT branch. Its only usage in the whole src tree is:

- `packages/core/src/lib/init.ts:119` — default value (`24 * 60 * 60`).
- `packages/core/src/lib/actions/session.ts:112–129` — the **database** strategy branch only.

There, it's the write-throttle: `sessionIsDueToBeUpdatedDate = session.expires - sessionMaxAge*1000 + updateAge*1000`, and `updateSession()` only fires if that's `<= Date.now()`. Even then, note that branch still always re-pushes the cookie `Set-Cookie` (lines 146–153) regardless of the throttle.

So `updateAge` throttles the **DB row write** for database sessions only. For JWT sessions it has zero effect — the cookie/JWT is rewritten unconditionally on each session read.

## For Ops

To cut cookie-rewrite frequency for JWT sessions, `session.updateAge` is the wrong knob (it does nothing there). The rewrite is intrinsic to the JWT branch re-signing the token each read (session.ts:72–79). Reducing writes would require code changes in that branch — e.g. only re-encoding when the remaining lifetime drops below a threshold — not a config change.

## Why you get `InvalidCheck`

The OAuth `state`/`pkce`/`nonce` checks are all stored in short-lived cookies, and **the TTL is hard-coded to 15 minutes** in three separate places. If the user lingers on Google's consent screen longer than that, the callback can't validate the check and `InvalidCheck` is thrown.

The relevant constants:

- `packages/core/src/lib/actions/callback/oauth/checks.ts:26` — `const COOKIE_TTL = 60 * 15 // 15 minutes`
- `packages/core/src/lib/actions/callback/oauth/checks.ts:149` — `const STATE_MAX_AGE = 60 * 15 // 15 minutes in seconds`
- `packages/core/src/lib/utils/cookie.ts:99,109,128` — the default `maxAge: 60 * 15` on the `state`, `pkceCodeVerifier`, and `webauthnChallenge` cookies.

## What actually times out

There are two independent 15-minute clocks, and either one produces `InvalidCheck`:

1. **The browser cookie expires.** `sealCookie` writes both a `maxAge` and an `expires` of now + 15 min (`checks.ts:36-37,55`). After that the browser simply stops sending the cookie. On callback, `parseCookie` hits `if (!value) throw new InvalidCheck(... cookie was missing)` (`checks.ts:68`), which is then re-wrapped by the enclosing `catch` as `InvalidCheck("<name> value could not be parsed", { cause: "<name> cookie was missing" })`.

2. **The sealed JWT's `exp` claim expires.** `sealCookie` encodes the envelope with `maxAge: COOKIE_TTL` (`checks.ts:48`), so the JWT carries `exp = now + 900s`. For `state` there's actually a *nested* JWT — the inner `encode({... maxAge: STATE_MAX_AGE ...})` at `checks.ts:174-179` — so state has two `exp` claims, both 15 min. `decode` calls `jose`'s `jwtDecrypt`, which validates `exp` by default (`jwt.ts:82-107`). Once past expiry it throws `JWTExpired`, the `catch` in `parseCookie` swallows it and re-throws `InvalidCheck("<name> value could not be parsed", { cause: JWTExpired })`.

So: sit >15 min and the cookie is gone (case 1); if the cookie is somehow still around, the encrypted `state`/`pkce`/`nonce` payload is expired (case 2). Note `decode` sets `clockTolerance: 15` (`jwt.ts:103`), so the practical cutoff is ~15 min + 15 s.

## Details worth knowing

- The checks are used in `handleOAuth`: `checks.state.use` → `checks.pkce.use` → `checks.nonce.use` (`oauth/callback.ts:130,152,230`), all going through `parseCookie`.
- The TTL is **not configurable** through the public options — `COOKIE_TTL`/`STATE_MAX_AGE` are module constants, and the cookie `maxAge` lives in `defaultCookies`. So there's no knob to raise the window for a slow consent flow today.
- The provider-id check (`checks.ts:77-81`) is a separate failure mode (created for a different provider), not time-related.

**Bottom line:** it's the fixed **15-minute** window applied both to the browser cookie's lifetime and to the sealed JWT expiration of the `state` (and its nested encrypted payload), plus `pkce`/`nonce`. Any consent-screen stay beyond ~15 min guarantees an expired/missing check cookie on return.

```

packages/core/src/lib/utils/cookie.ts:109  state:            maxAge: 60 * 15
packages/core/src/lib/utils/cookie.ts:128  webauthnChallenge: maxAge: 60 * 15
```

## 3. The extra nested JWT for `state` — `checks.ts:149`

```
packages/core/src/lib/actions/callback/oauth/checks.ts:149
  const STATE_MAX_AGE = 60 * 15 // 15 minutes in seconds
```

|---|---|---|---|
| `state` | 15 min (`COOKIE_TTL` / `cookie.ts:109`) | 15 min (`COOKIE_TTL`) | 15 min (`STATE_MAX_AGE`) |
| `pkce` | 15 min (`COOKIE_TTL` / `cookie.ts:99`) | 15 min (`COOKIE_TTL`) | — |

## What times out

The OAuth "check" cookies that Auth.js sets when the sign‑in is *initiated*, and the encrypted JWTs sealed inside them. Everything is fixed at **15 minutes**:

- `packages/core/src/lib/actions/callback/oauth/checks.ts:26` → `const COOKIE_TTL = 60 * 15`
- `.../utils/cookie.ts` → the default cookie options for `state`, `pkceCodeVerifier`, and `nonce` also carry `maxAge: 60 * 15`
- `checks.ts:149` → `STATE_MAX_AGE = 60 * 15` (the JWT *inside* the state cookie)

At sign‑in, `authorization-url.ts` creates three checks — `checks.state.create`, `checks.pkce.create`, `checks.nonce.create` — which write `authjs.state`, `authjs.pkce.code_verifier`, and `authjs.nonce`. `sealCookie` (`checks.ts:29`) encrypts the payload with `maxAge: COOKIE_TTL` **and** sets the cookie's `expires` to now + 15 min. So the cookie is valid for 15 minutes from the moment the sign‑in starts, not from when the user returns.

## Why lingering on Google's consent screen produces `InvalidCheck`

When the user finally comes back, the callback runs `handleOAuth` → `checks.state.use` (then `pkce.use`, then `nonce.use`). Each calls `parseCookie` (`checks.ts:59`), which fails in one of two ways once 15 minutes have elapsed:

1. **Browser already dropped the expired cookie** → `if (!value) throw new InvalidCheck(`${name} cookie was missing`)` (`checks.ts:68`).
2. **Cookie still sent but its sealed JWT has expired** → `decode` calls jose's `jwtDecrypt`, which throws `JWTExpired` (only ~15s `clockTolerance`, `jwt.ts:103`) → caught by the surrounding `try/catch`, which re‑throws `InvalidCheck(`${name} value could not be parsed`, { cause: error })` (`checks.ts:83`).

Since `state.use` is evaluated first in `handleOAuth` (`oauth/callback.ts:130`), the user typically surfaces the state‑flavored `InvalidCheck`. Google has all three checks enabled, so `pkce`/`nonce` would fail the same way if state were somehow fine.

One more place the same constant bites: on the redirect‑proxy path, `state.decode` (`checks.ts:191`, called from `callback/index.ts:72`) decodes the state JWT directly, and its 15‑minute `STATE_MAX_AGE` expiry will also throw `InvalidCheck("State could not be decoded")`.

## Bottom line

Nothing about Google is special — the 15‑minute window is a hardcoded constant (`COOKIE_TTL`) on the pending‑OAuth cookies/JWTs. If a user idles on the consent screen longer than that, the state/pkce/nonce check material is gone by the time the callback fires, and `parseCookie` converts the expired/missing cookie into an `InvalidCheck`. There's no config knob for it; raising `COOKIE_TTL` (and the cookie `maxAge`s) is what would need to change.

## Where the timeout is defined

It comes from **two** layered places, both in `packages/core/src/lib/actions/callback/oauth/checks.ts`:

**1. The sealed JWT + the cookie's `expires` — one constant, shared by every check**

```ts
const COOKIE_TTL = 60 * 15 // 15 minutes        // checks.ts:26
```

`sealCookie` (`checks.ts:29`) is the single choke point every check flows through, and it applies `COOKIE_TTL` twice:

```ts
const expires = new Date()
expires.setTime(expires.getTime() + COOKIE_TTL * 1000)   // checks.ts:36-37
...
const encoded = await encode({ ...options.jwt, maxAge: COOKIE_TTL, ... })  // checks.ts:48
const cookieOptions = { ...cookie.options, expires }      // checks.ts:55
```

So both the encrypted payload's `exp` and the cookie's `expires` are set from `COOKIE_TTL`.

**2. The default cookie `maxAge` attribute — declared per‑cookie, and *not* uniform**

In `packages/core/src/lib/utils/cookie.ts`, only some checks declare their own 15‑minute `maxAge`:

| check | cookie name | default `maxAge: 60*15` in cookie.ts? |
|---|---|---|
| PKCE | `authjs.pkce.code_verifier` | ✅ line 99 |
| state | `authjs.state` | ✅ line 109 |
| nonce | `authjs.nonce` | ❌ *(no maxAge — lines 112‑120)* |
| WebAuthn | `authjs.challenge` | ✅ line 128 |

There's also `STATE_MAX_AGE = 60 * 15` (`checks.ts:149`), but that governs the *inner* state JWT used by `state.decode` on the redirect‑proxy path — a separate encode from the cookie's `COOKIE_TTL`.

## Does it cover state, PKCE and nonce alike?

**Effectively yes — all three expire after 15 minutes — but the mechanism differs slightly for `nonce`.**

- **state and PKCE** are covered redundantly: `sealCookie`'s `COOKIE_TTL` (JWT `exp` + cookie `expires`) *and* their own `maxAge: 60*15` default in `cookie.ts`.
- **nonce** has no `maxAge` default in `cookie.ts`, so it is covered **only** by `sealCookie` — i.e. the cookie's `expires` (set at `checks.ts:55`) plus the sealed JWT's 15‑minute `maxAge`. The end result is the same 15‑minute window; it just doesn't get the extra `Max-Age` attribute that state/PKCE do.

So the practical outcome is identical for all three: 15 minutes from when the sign‑in started. The one asymmetry worth flagging is that `nonce` relies entirely on `sealCookie`'s `expires`/JWT expiry, whereas state and PKCE have the timeout asserted in two independent spots (`checks.ts` and `cookie.ts`) — so if someone ever changed `COOKIE_TTL`, nonce would follow automatically along with the others, but the cookie.ts defaults for state/PKCE would no longer match it.

`packages/core/src/lib/actions/callback/oauth/checks.ts:26`
```ts
const COOKIE_TTL = 60 * 15 // 15 minutes
```

`sealCookie` (checks.ts:29–57) applies that TTL **twice**:
- the browser cookie `expires` is set to `now + COOKIE_TTL` (line 36–37), and
- the sealed JWT payload is encoded with `maxAge: COOKIE_TTL` (line 48).

The state token even has a redundant second layer: `state.create` wraps the payload in a JWT with `STATE_MAX_AGE = 60 * 15` (checks.ts:149, 178) before sealing it again.

When the user returns from Google's consent screen, `handleOAuth` consumes the checks:

`packages/core/src/lib/actions/callback/oauth/callback.ts:130, 152, 230`
```ts
const state = await checks.state.use(cookies, resCookies, options)
...
const codeVerifier = await checks.pkce.use(cookies, resCookies, options)
...
expectedNonce: await checks.nonce.use(cookies, resCookies, options),
```

Each `use` goes through `parseCookie` (checks.ts:59–88):

- If the browser already discarded the expired cookie → `InvalidCheck("<name> cookie was missing")` (line 68).
- If the cookie is still present but its JWT has expired, `decode` calls jose's `jwtDecrypt`, which validates `exp` and throws `JWTExpired`. That's caught and re-wrapped as `InvalidCheck("<name> value could not be parsed")` (line 83–87).

(In redirect-proxy mode, `callback/index.ts:72` hits the inner state JWT instead, giving `InvalidCheck("State could not be decoded")`, checks.ts:202.)

`InvalidCheck` is a client-safe error type (`packages/core/src/errors.ts:12, 245`), so `packages/core/src/index.ts:177–196` catches it and redirects the user to the error page with `?error=InvalidCheck`.

```ts
const COOKIE_TTL = 60 * 15 // 15 minutes
```

```ts
expires.setTime(expires.getTime() + COOKIE_TTL * 1000)   // line 37 → browser cookie `expires`
...
const encoded = await encode({
```

waypoints.summary:
Users who sit on Google's consent screen >15 min hit InvalidCheck on callback. Root cause is the OAuth check cookies (state/pkceCodeVerifier/nonce), not the authorization code or session.

Three hardcoded 15-min caps in packages/core/src/lib/actions/callback/oauth/checks.ts:
- COOKIE_TTL = 60*15 sets both the cookie `expires` and the sealed JWT `maxAge` in sealCookie (lines 26, 36-37, 48).
- STATE_MAX_AGE = 60*15 for the inner state payload (lines 149, 178).
- Reinforced by default maxAge: 60*15 in defaultCookies for pkceCodeVerifier/state/webauthnChallenge (packages/core/src/lib/utils/cookie.ts:99,109,128).

Failure modes on callback via useCookie -> parseCookie:
1. Cookie dropped by browser -> InvalidCheck("{name} cookie was missing") (checks.ts:68).
2. Cookie present but JWT exp passed -> jwtDecrypt throws JWTExpired (only clockTolerance:15s, jwt.ts:103) -> rethrown InvalidCheck("{name} value could not be parsed") (checks.ts:84).
3. state.decode fails first with InvalidCheck("State could not be decoded") from STATE_MAX_AGE.

Key constraint for any fix: NOT user-configurable today. COOKIE_TTL is a module constant, not read from options.cookies, and sealCookie passes its own maxAge to encode. Bumping cookies.state.options.maxAge extends only the browser cookie (Max-Age beats Expires per RFC 6265) but the inner JWT exp stays at 15 min, so parseCookie still fails with JWTExpired. Real fix must source COOKIE_TTL and STATE_MAX_AGE from options.

Here's what's going on, and what to tell the reviewer.

## What `trustHost` actually does

`trustHost` isn't a hardening knob — it's a **required-on switch**. In `packages/core/src/lib/utils/assert.ts:96`, every request runs through `assertConfig`, which does:

```ts
if (!options.trustHost) {
  return new UntrustedHost(`Host must be trusted. URL was: ${request.url}`)
}
```

So if `trustHost` is falsy, Auth.js throws `UntrustedHost` on **every** request. Setting `trustHost: false` doesn't lock anything down — it takes the app offline.

## Where the default comes from

`packages/core/src/lib/utils/env.ts:44`:

```ts
config.trustHost ??= !!(
  envObject.AUTH_URL ??
  envObject.AUTH_TRUST_HOST ??
  envObject.VERCEL ??
  envObject.CF_PAGES ??
  envObject.NODE_ENV !== "production"
)
```

It defaults to `true` when `AUTH_URL` is set, on Vercel/Cloudflare Pages, or in any non-production env. The framework adapters also force it on (`frameworks-qwik`, `frameworks-solid-start`, `frameworks-sveltekit`).

## The security story

`trustHost: true` means Auth.js will honor the proxy-provided `X-Forwarded-Host` / `X-Forwarded-Proto` headers (see `createActionURL` in `env.ts:94` and the docs in `migrating-to-v5.mdx`) to auto-detect the URL when `AUTH_URL` isn't set. The actual hardening moves are:

1. **Set `AUTH_URL` explicitly** — when it's set, `createActionURL` uses it and ignores the forwarded-host headers entirely, so the host is no longer attacker-influenced.
2. **Set a strong `AUTH_SECRET`** (also required, per the `MissingSecret` check).
3. **Strip/normalize `X-Forwarded-*` at the edge** so untrusted clients can't inject them.

Setting `trustHost: false` does none of this; it just trips the `UntrustedHost` guard.

## What to tell them

`trustHost: false` is not a hardening flag — it's a kill switch. In this codebase it's the exact condition that makes `assertConfig` reject every request with `UntrustedHost`, and it defaults to `true` in dev, on Vercel/CF Pages, and whenever `AUTH_URL` is set. The correct hardening is to pin `AUTH_URL` (which makes Auth.js stop trusting `X-Forwarded-Host`/`X-Forwarded-Proto`), set a strong `AUTH_SECRET`, and sanitize forwarded headers at the proxy.

## Short answer: don't do it — that's not a hardening knob, it's a functional break.

Here's what the code actually does:

**`trustHost` is not a security control.** It only decides whether Auth.js is allowed to derive the app's URL from the `host` header (and `X-Forwarded-Host` / `X-Forwarded-Proto` behind a proxy). It has no bearing on sessions, cookies, CSRF, or authorization.

**`false` is a hard failure, not a mitigation.** In `packages/core/src/lib/utils/assert.ts:96`:

```ts
if (!options.trustHost) {
  return new UntrustedHost(`Host must be trusted. URL was: ${request.url}`)
}
```

Every request returns a `ConfigError` before init. So `trustHost: false` doesn't harden the config — it makes the app 100% non-functional.

**Setting it explicitly is strictly worse than the default.** From `packages/core/src/lib/utils/env.ts:44`, the default is already conditional:

```ts
config.trustHost ??= !!(
  envObject.AUTH_URL ?? envObject.AUTH_TRUST_HOST ?? envObject.VERCEL ??
  envObject.CF_PAGES ?? envObject.NODE_ENV !== "production"
)
```

Note `??=`: an explicit `trustHost: false` *overrides* this and pins it off even in dev/Vercel/Cloudflare/`AUTH_URL` setups that would otherwise work. In production without `AUTH_URL`/`AUTH_TRUST_HOST`, the default already evaluates to `false` — so you get the strict behaviour for free, and an explicit `false` only removes your ability to opt in via env at deploy time.

**The real hardening for host-header injection** is to pin the canonical URL and only trust forwarding headers from a proxy you control:
- Set `AUTH_URL` (or `AUTH_SECRET`) so the URL is never derived from an untrusted header — `AUTH_URL` alone makes `trustHost` default to `true` but makes the derived host irrelevant.
- Keep `trustHost: true` (or `AUTH_TRUST_HOST=true`) only where a trusted reverse proxy terminates the request.

So the reviewer's intent (prevent attacker-controlled `Host` from poisoning redirect/callback URLs) is legitimate, but the mechanism is wrong. Tell them to configure `AUTH_URL` and rely on the environment-conditional default, rather than hardcoding `trustHost: false`.

ANSWER: trust_host=true; reason=trustHost only gates URL derivation from the Host header, so setting it false triggers UntrustedHost on every request instead of hardening anything — pin `AUTH_URL` behind a trusted proxy and let the env-conditional default stand.

```ts
const url = process.env.AUTH_URL ?? process.env.NEXTAUTH_URL
if (!url) return
const { pathname } = new URL(url)
if (pathname === "/") return
config.basePath ||= pathname      // line 29: derive from AUTH_URL/NEXTAUTH_URL
...
} finally {
  config.basePath ||= "/api/auth"  // line 34: next-auth's default
  coreSetEnvDefaults(process.env, config, true)
}
```

So next-auth's precedence is: `config.basePath` → pathname of `AUTH_URL`/`NEXTAUTH_URL` → **`/api/auth`** (line 34). The `/api/auth` default is deliberately next-auth-specific for backwards compat; every other Auth.js integration defaults to `/auth`.

**The generic core default** — `packages/core/src/lib/utils/env.ts:30`: `config.basePath ??= "/auth"`. next-auth calls this via `coreSetEnvDefaults(..., true)` (the `true` = `suppressBasePathWarning`), after it has already pinned `/api/auth`, so the core default never wins for next-auth.

**Call site** — `packages/next-auth/src/index.ts`: `NextAuth()` runs `setEnvDefaults` on the config (line 408 for a static config; 382/389/393/398/403 for the lazy `(req) => config` form), so your `basePath: "/auth/v2"` is picked up there and consumed by `createActionURL()` (`packages/core/src/lib/utils/env.ts:73-113`).

```ts
signinUrl:   `${url}/signin/${id}`,
```

Default cookie names live in **`packages/core/src/lib/utils/cookie.ts`**, in the exported `defaultCookies(useSecureCookies: boolean)` function (lines 59–132).

For your session cookie specifically:

```ts
sessionToken: {
  name: `${cookiePrefix}authjs.session-token`,   // cookiePrefix = "__Secure-" when secure
  options: { httpOnly: true, sameSite: "lax", path: "/", secure: useSecureCookies },
}
```

So the default is `authjs.session-token`, or `__Secure-authjs.session-token` over HTTPS. All other cookies are defined in the same object: `callbackUrl` (`authjs.callback-url`), `csrfToken` (`authjs.csrf-token`, with a `__Host-` prefix when secure), `pkceCodeVerifier` (`authjs.pkce.code_verifier`), `state` (`authjs.state`), `nonce` (`authjs.nonce`), and `webauthnChallenge` (`authjs.challenge`).

How your override works:
- `init.ts:107-112` merges `cookie.defaultCookies(...)` with `config.cookies`, so your `cookies.sessionToken.name: "acme_sid"` wins over the default.
- One driver of the prefix is `config.useSecureCookies ?? url.protocol === "https:"` at `init.ts:108-110` — the merge means your override replaces the whole `sessionToken` object, so the `__Secure-` prefix won't be added to `acme_sid` regardless.
- On the read side, `jwt.ts:152` also falls back to `defaultCookies(secureCookie ?? false).sessionToken.name` when no cookie name is passed, so if any code path constructs a `SessionStore`/`getToken` without an explicit name it would expect the default name, not `acme_sid`. Worth verifying your call sites pass the cookie name through the config rather than relying on that fallback — otherwise the edge stripping the default-named cookie plus a fallback read could break token decoding.

For the CDN constraint: since the allowlist can't hold wildcards or prefixes, note the other Auth.js cookies (`authjs.csrf-token`, etc.) will also be stripped at the edge unless you rename them too, which would break CSRF/PKCE/state flows on OAuth callbacks.

Understood — `acme_sid` is the one name that survives, and the CDN list is out of your control. That locks in a few consequences worth stating plainly, because they're not just cosmetic:

**1. The other Auth.js cookies will not survive the edge.** Defaults in `cookie.ts` are `authjs.csrf-token`, `authjs.callback-url`, `authjs.state`, `authjs.pkce.code_verifier`, `authjs.nonce`, `authjs.challenge`. If the edge strips everything but `acme_sid`, then origin-side:
- CSRF checks fail (`csrfToken` cookie absent on POST to signin/signout/callback).
- OAuth `state` + `pkceCodeVerifier` fail on the callback (they're set before redirect, must return after).
- `callbackUrl` is dropped, so post-login redirect falls back.

So a stateless JWT session having a working name isn't enough — the interactive sign-in paths need those cookies. Either those requests bypass the edge (dedicated hostname/path/port for the auth routes, or direct-to-origin), or OAuth sign-in breaks.

**2. Chunking collides with the allowlist.** `SessionStore` splits a session value larger than ~3936 bytes into `${name}.0`, `${name}.1`, … (`cookie.ts:180-204`). Those are distinct cookie names — `acme_sid.0` won't match an exact-name allowlist entry and will be stripped, silently truncating the session. Keep the JWT small (few claims, no big user objects) or use `strategy: "database"` so the cookie holds only an opaque token.

**3. Prod secure-prefix conflict.** `init.ts:108-110` computes `useSecureCookies` from `url.protocol === "https:"`. Your override replaces the whole `sessionToken` object, so `acme_sid` won't get `__Secure-` — which is fine per the allowlist, but it does mean you should still set `options.secure: true` explicitly so the cookie is HTTPS-only in prod.

Net: the rename is necessary but not sufficient. The open question is where the auth endpoints sit relative to the edge — if they're behind it too, this constraint blocks OAuth/CSRF entirely, not just the session cookie.

```ts
from: "Auth.js <no-reply@authjs.dev>",
```

So the default sender is `Auth.js <no-reply@authjs.dev>` (line 10), which fails DMARC alignment for `acme.dev` — hence the override. It's used directly in the request body as `from: provider.from` (line 22). Also note `maxAge` is defaulted to 24h on line 11 there.

Sounds right — but one nuance worth confirming with ops, because "added that address to SPF/DKIM" is a common over-claim:

DMARC alignment is **domain-level, not address-level**, and it only checks the domain that actually authenticated:

- **SPF** authenticates the *envelope* sender (MAIL FROM / Return-Path), not the visible `From:`. That envelope for Resend mail is Resend's own bounce domain (or a verified subdomain) — never `login@acme.dev`. You can't put a mailbox address in SPF; you publish a record for a *domain*. So if ops just added `login@acme.dev` to an SPF policy, that alone does nothing for alignment.
- **DKIM** is what usually saves you here. Resend signs with `d=<the domain you verified in Resend>`. For relaxed alignment against the visible `From: ...@acme.dev`, the domain **acme.dev must be verified in Resend** (i.e. the DKIM record Resend hands you is published at acme.dev). If they instead verified some Resend-provisioned domain, DKIM won't align either and the Gmail/Outlook bounce returns.

So the thing to double-check: `acme.dev` is the domain verified in the Resend dashboard, and the DKIM record Resend shows is the one published. The SPF side is about the envelope/bounce domain, which is arguably what they meant, but "login@acme.dev" is the wrong unit for it.

On the code side nothing changes — `from: provider.from` (resend.ts:22) just echoes whatever you pass, so your `Resend({ from: "Acme <login@acme.dev>" })` override is all that's needed there.

```ts

```

That default is what `sendVerificationRequest` reads here (`packages/core/src/providers/resend.ts:22`):

```ts
body: JSON.stringify({
  from: provider.from,   // Auth.js <no-reply@authjs.dev> unless overridden
  ...
})
```

So the provider's default `from` is `Auth.js <no-reply@authjs.dev>`, which is why your Gmail/Outlook bounces happen (`no-reply@authjs.dev` ≠ `acme.dev` → DMARC fails alignment). Setting `from: "login@acme.dev"` (or `"Acme <login@acme.dev>"`) in the `Resend({...})` config flows through `options: config` and overrides line 10. Worth confirming the merged config actually wins — `options` is spread at line 33, but note it's nested under `options`, not spread at the top level, so verify how `provider.from` resolves against your override in this fork.

One clarification worth nailing down, because the wording matters here.

"That sender" is ambiguous between two things:

- The **default** I quoted: `Auth.js <no-reply@authjs.dev>`. Ops cannot put this in your SPF/DKIM — `authjs.dev` isn't your domain, and no amount of your DNS records will make it align with `acme.dev`. If this is what you meant, that's a false premise.
- The **override** you configured: `login@acme.dev`. This is the one ops would add to acme.dev's SPF/DKIM, and it's the only one of the two that can pass DMARC alignment. I'll assume this is what you meant.

Also confirming my earlier caveat was unfounded: `parseProviders` (`packages/core/src/lib/utils/providers.ts:32-39`) pulls `options` off the provider and does `merge(defaults, userOptions, {...})`, so `userOptions` wins — your `from` override does take effect over the line-10 default. Nothing nested/stuck.

Two things to double-check on your side while ops has the DNS open:

1. **Alignment type.** If your records are DKIM-signed for `acme.dev` but you send from a subdomain, you need either `login@acme.dev` with relaxed DMARC (`adkim=r`) or DKIM keyed on whatever subdomain. Since `login@acme.dev` is on the bare domain, this is fine as long as the DKIM selector covers `acme.dev`.
2. **Resend's own envelope sender.** Resend sends `Return-Path`/envelope-from from *its* return-path domain. `From:` alignment is what DMARC checks, but SPF is evaluated against the envelope domain, so SPF passing is on Resend's domain, not yours — your `login@acme.dev` entry in SPF only matters if you're also sending via your own MTA. Make sure you're not expecting the SPF record alone to cover Resend traffic.

If instead you meant login@acme.dev and ops added *that exact address* to both SPF and DKIM, you're aligned. Which did you mean?

replies:
**`packages/core/src/providers/resend.ts`** — inside the `Resend` factory:

- Line 10: `from: "Auth.js <no-reply@authjs.dev>"` — the default sender. This is the value that fails DMARC alignment for your domain, and it's what the request body uses at line 22 (`from: provider.from`). Passing `from: "login@acme.dev"` in `EmailUserConfig` replaces it.
- Line 11: `maxAge: 24 * 60 * 60` — the other default (magic-link token lifetime).

Both are only defaults: `options: config` (line 33) means user-supplied config wins in the merged provider object. Note the same `from` default is repeated in every email provider (e.g. `sendgrid.ts`, `nodemailer.ts`), so the shared override path is per-provider config rather than a single global.

Good — one clarification worth pinning, since SPF/DKIM are domain-scoped, not mailbox-scoped:

- **DKIM**: this is the alignment leg that actually carries you. `login@acme.dev` signs with `d=acme.dev`, which aligns with the From domain. As long as the key Resend generated is the one published at `resend._domainkey.acme.dev`, that leg is solid and Gmail/Outlook will accept it.
- **SPF**: evaluated against the envelope `Return-Path`, not the visible `From`. Resend sets that themselves (typically their own bounce subdomain, e.g. `send.acme.dev` or an amazonses-style host). So "we added the sender to SPF" only helps if what's in your `acme.dev` TXT record actually covers Resend's sending infrastructure *and* their envelope domain is one you control. If the Return-Path is on Resend's domain, SPF aligns to *them*, not to you — and you're passing purely on DKIM. That's fine and normal (DMARC needs only one aligned leg), but it means the SPF edit may be doing nothing for deliverability, and a broken DKIM key would take you back to bounces with no SPF fallback.
- Docs corroborate the prerequisite: the sending domain must be added/verified in the Resend account, and that domain is the one in the `from` option (`docs/pages/getting-started/providers/resend.mdx:36`). `login@acme.dev` in `Resend({ from })` satisfies that.

Two things I'd verify rather than assume: what Resend reports as the Return-Path for a live send (send a magic-link to a mail-tester/`check-auth` address and read the received headers), and that the DKIM selector published is the one Resend is actually signing with. If DKIM is the only aligned leg, you want it verified before you trust the setup.

I dropped a waypoint recording the sender decision and the per-provider-default trap, so a future provider swap doesn't silently reintroduce the bounce.

```ts
config.secret ??= process.env.AUTH_SECRET ?? process.env.NEXTAUTH_SECRET
```


Framework layers just choose the env object passed to the same function: `process.env` (express `packages/frameworks-express/src/index.ts:167,184`; next-auth `packages/next-auth/src/index.ts:408`), `req.env` (qwik `:165`), `platform.env`/`event.platform.env` (sveltekit `packages/frameworks-sveltekit/src/lib/env.ts:6`, called at `index.ts:328`), solid-start `process.env` (`packages/frameworks-solid-start/src/index.ts:245,268`).

1. **Your explicit pass is the only reason this works, and it does work.** Env is a *fallback*, never an override: core only fills from env when `!config.secret?.length`, next-auth uses `??=`. **Where it would actually come back, and the fix:** the real risk isn't malice, it's a stale hint that makes the stock name look like the supported path:
- `turbo.json:43` — `AUTH_SECRET` sits in the `test:e2e` env list. It's dead now (nobody sets it), which is exactly how it gets resurrected: someone hits a e2e failure, sees the name, and sets it. Drop it or swap to `ACME_AUTH_SECRET`.

- Examples (`apps/examples/solid-start/src/env/schema.ts:9` zod-requires it, the docker-compose hardcoded value): upstream-facing, leave them.

**Enforcement should fail at deploy, not at first request.** Auth.js's only guard is `assertConfig` → `MissingSecret("Please define a `secret`")` at `packages/core/src/lib/utils/assert.ts:100-101`, thrown per-request. If someone replaces your explicit prop with the env route, prod throws on the first auth request — fail-closed, but long after the deploy that introduced it. And it can't distinguish "prop missing" from "env missing," so the error won't point at the ACME_ mismatch.

So two concrete guards, both cheap:
1. A `check:env` script wired into `pnpm lint` scanning only `apps/**` + deploy manifests (k8s/Docker/compose/env files) for assignments of `AUTH_SECRET`, `NEXTAUTH_SECRET`, or `AUTH_SECRET_1..3`, with `packages/**` and `docs/**` allowlisted.
2. A boot-time assertion in each service that `process.env.ACME_AUTH_SECRET` is non-empty, so the ACME_/stock divergence fails at deploy time with a message naming ACME_.

**Auth.js never looks at `ACME_AUTH_SECRET`.** There is no `ACME_` string anywhere in this repo. The only place the core library consults the environment for a secret is `setEnvDefaults`:

`packages/core/src/lib/utils/env.ts:33-41`
```ts
if (!config.secret?.length) {
  config.secret = []
  const secret = envObject.AUTH_SECRET
  if (secret) config.secret.push(secret)
  for (const i of [1, 2, 3]) {
    const secret = envObject[`AUTH_SECRET_${i}`]
    if (secret) config.secret.unshift(secret)
  }
}
```

So the recognized names are:
- `AUTH_SECRET` (primary)
- `AUTH_SECRET_1`, `AUTH_SECRET_2`, `AUTH_SECRET_3` (rotation keys, prepended so they take precedence)
- plus `NEXTAUTH_SECRET` as a legacy fallback, but only in the `next-auth` wrapper: `packages/next-auth/src/lib/env.ts:24` → `config.secret ??= process.env.AUTH_SECRET ?? process.env.NEXTAUTH_SECRET`

Which env object gets passed in depends on the integration: Next.js passes `process.env` (`packages/next-auth/src/index.ts:382`), SvelteKit passes its platform `env` (`packages/frameworks-sveltekit/src/lib/index.ts:328`), Qwik passes `req.env` and does `env.get("AUTH_SECRET")` (`packages/frameworks-qwik/src/index.ts:325,353`), Express/`apps/proxy` pass `process.env`.

That works: the `if (!config.secret?.length)` guard means env lookup is skipped entirely once `secret` is populated.

```ts
cookies: merge(
```

**Why.** In a cross-site iframe, the "site for cookies" is the *partner's* site, not yours. So *every* request your app makes from inside the frame — including same-origin `fetch`es to `/api/auth/*` and the top-level-ish callback navigations — is cross-site. `SameSite=Lax` cookies get withheld there. |---|---|---|

| `callbackUrl` | `pages/index.ts` | post-signin redirect target lost |

So the practical config is closer to:

```ts
const crossSite = { sameSite: "none", secure: true } as const
cookies: {
  sessionToken:      { options: crossSite },
  csrfToken:         { options: crossSite },
  callbackUrl:       { options: crossSite },
  state:             { options: crossSite },
  nonce:             { options: crossSite },
  pkceCodeVerifier:  { options: crossSite },
}
```

## How Auth.js derives its own URL

The single source of truth is **`createActionURL`** in `packages/core/src/lib/utils/env.ts:73`. Every signin/signout/callback/session URL is built through it, and it has two branches:

**1. Env URL wins (your case).** If `AUTH_URL` (or legacy `NEXTAUTH_URL`) is set, request headers are never consulted:

```ts
const envUrl = envObject.AUTH_URL ?? envObject.NEXTAUTH_URL
if (envUrl) {
  url = new URL(envUrl)          // origin taken straight from AUTH_URL
  // basePath mismatch handling…
}
```

The `basePath` and `action` are then appended (`env.ts:107-112`), so pinning `AUTH_URL=https://app.acme.dev` makes every callback URL absolute to that origin regardless of what the request looks like.

**2. Header detection fallback (when no `AUTH_URL`).** This is the path that broke for you:

```ts
const detectedHost = headers.get("x-forwarded-host") ?? headers.get("host")
const detectedProtocol = headers.get("x-forwarded-proto") ?? protocol ?? "https"
url = new URL(`${_protocol}//${detectedHost}`)
```

(`env.ts:94-101`) Since your ingress strips `x-forwarded-host`/`x-forwarded-proto`, it falls to `host` — the pod's internal address — exactly the symptom you saw.

## Why the env var also fixed the trust check

`createActionURL` is only reached after `assertConfig` passes, and `assertConfig` bails with `UntrustedHost` unless `config.trustHost` is true (`packages/core/src/lib/utils/assert.ts:96`). `setEnvDefaults` auto-enables `trustHost` when any of these are present (`env.ts:44-50`):

```ts
config.trustHost ??= !!(
  envObject.AUTH_URL ?? envObject.AUTH_TRUST_HOST ??
  envObject.VERCEL ?? envObject.CF_PAGES ??
  envObject.NODE_ENV !== "production"
)
```

So setting `AUTH_URL` both supplies the origin *and* implicitly satisfies `trustHost`. (Setting only `AUTH_TRUST_HOST=true` would have trusted the headers — but with forwarded headers stripped, that would still have resolved to the pod address.)

## The Next.js wrapper layer

`next-auth` adds two things on top (v4-compat):

- `reqWithEnvURL` (`packages/next-auth/src/lib/env.ts:7-13`) rewrites an incoming `NextRequest`'s origin to the `AUTH_URL` origin before it ever hits core.
- `setEnvDefaults` (`env.ts:22-37`) derives `basePath` from the `AUTH_URL` pathname (defaulting to `/api/auth`), and RPC-style server calls like `getSession` (`packages/next-auth/src/lib/index.ts:62-70`) call `createActionURL` directly with `process.env`.

Net: `AUTH_URL` short-circuits header-based inference at the top of the chain, which is the intended escape hatch for exactly the "proxy strips forwarded headers" topology you're on.

Understood — no headers, no platform team. Pinning `AUTH_URL` is the supported answer here, not a hack to retire later.

Two things worth keeping straight so it stays solid:

- **Don't also set `AUTH_TRUST_HOST` expecting it to help.** With forwarded headers stripped, trusting them just gets you the pod address again. `AUTH_URL` is what makes `trustHost` true implicitly anyway (`env.ts:44-50`).
- **Keep the path consistent.** If `AUTH_URL=https://app.acme.dev` (no path) and your `basePath` is the default `/api/auth`, that's fine. If you ever put a path in `AUTH_URL`, it must match `basePath` or you'll get the `env-url-basepath-mismatch` warning and a silently reset pathname (`env.ts:86-92`).

That's the whole mechanism — one env var, headers never consulted.

replies:
Two separate mechanisms are in play — one for the URL it *detects*, one for the URL it *serves actions from*.

**1. Header-based auto-detection (`createActionURL`)**

`packages/core/src/lib/utils/env.ts:73` is the override-aware version used by framework adapters (e.g. `getSession` in `packages/next-auth/src/lib/index.ts:63`):

```ts
const envUrl = envObject.AUTH_URL ?? envObject.NEXTAUTH_URL
if (envUrl) { url = new URL(envUrl) ... }
else {
  const detectedHost = headers.get("x-forwarded-host") ?? headers.get("host")
  const detectedProtocol = headers.get("x-forwarded-proto") ?? protocol ?? "https"
  url = new URL(`${_protocol}//${detectedHost}`)
}
```

So precedence is: `AUTH_URL` → `NEXTAUTH_URL` → `x-forwarded-host` → `host`. Your ingress strips the `x-forwarded-*` pair, so detection fell through to `host` — the pod's internal address. That's exactly the callback-URL symptom you saw. Nothing in Auth.js can recover the public host without either the forwarded headers or an explicit env URL.

**2. `config.url` for the actual action / callback resolution**

Inside core, `toInternalRequest` (`packages/core/src/lib/utils/web.ts:38`) just does `new URL(req.url)` and that becomes `options.url`; everything downstream (`createCallbackUrl` → `url.origin`, the OAuth `redirect_uri`, error/sign-in page redirects) derives from it. So the caller has to hand core a Request whose URL is already the public one.

For Next.js that rewrite is `reqWithEnvURL` (`packages/next-auth/src/lib/env.ts:7`):

```ts
const url = process.env.AUTH_URL ?? process.env.NEXTAUTH_URL
if (!url) return req
const { origin: envOrigin } = new URL(url)
const { href, origin } = req.nextUrl
return new NextRequest(href.replace(origin, envOrigin), req)
```

Without `AUTH_URL` it returns `req` untouched, and Next reconstructs that URL from the `host` header — same dead end.

**Side effects worth knowing about your fix**

- `setEnvDefaults` (`env.ts:44`) sets `trustHost ??= !!(AUTH_URL ?? AUTH_TRUST_HOST ?? VERCEL ?? CF_PAGES ?? NODE_ENV !== "production")`. So setting `AUTH_URL` also implicitly opted you into `trustHost: true`, which is what stops `assertConfig` from returning `UntrustedHost` (`lib/utils/assert.ts:96`). One env var closed both holes.
- With `AUTH_URL=https://app.acme.dev` (pathname `/`), `next-auth`'s `setEnvDefaults` leaves `basePath` at `/api/auth` (`packages/next-auth/src/lib/env.ts:27-34`). Core's own `setEnvDefaults` requires `new URL(url).pathname` to be non-`/` before adopting it as basePath, so a bare origin doesn't accidentally become your base path.
- If you ever add a path (`https://app.acme.dev/auth`) *and* set `basePath` in config, you'll get `env-url-basepath-redundant`, or `env-url-basepath-mismatch` when the two disagree (`warnings.ts:9-11`, `env.ts:86-92`).

Understood — headers are off the table permanently, not a thing to re-raise with the platform team. It's recorded as a hard constraint on my side.

For anything URL-shaped from here on, the working assumption is: `AUTH_URL=https://app.acme.dev` is the single source of truth for the public origin, and any new concern (extra path, redirect proxy, provider callback paths) gets solved inside Auth.js config or the app — never by asking the ingress to forward more headers.

One thing I'd flag as adjacent rather than a rehash: `AUTH_URL` fixes the *URL Auth.js computes*, but any URL you construct yourself in app code (e.g. building a callback path by hand, or email links in a provider's `sendVerificationRequest`) still needs that same origin — those won't pick it up automatically. If that comes up, the fix is reading `AUTH_URL` in your code, not touching the proxy.

## How Auth.js resolves its own URL

The single source of truth is `createActionURL()` in `packages/core/src/lib/utils/env.ts` (exported from `@auth/core`). Given an action (`signin`, `callback`, `session`, …), protocol, request `headers`, env object, and config, it decides the base URL with a **strict precedence**:

```ts
const envUrl = envObject.AUTH_URL ?? envObject.NEXTAUTH_URL

if (envUrl) {
  url = new URL(envUrl)              // 1. configured URL wins outright
  // reconcile basePath (warns env-url-basepath-mismatch / -redundant)
} else {
  const detectedHost = headers.get("x-forwarded-host") ?? headers.get("host")   // 2. forwarded host, else host
  const detectedProtocol = headers.get("x-forwarded-proto") ?? protocol ?? "https"
  url = new URL(`${_protocol}//${detectedHost}`)
}
// then append basePath + action
```

So:

1. **`AUTH_URL` / `NEXTAUTH_URL`** — if set, it is used verbatim; header detection is skipped entirely. Its `pathname` becomes `config.basePath` unless `basePath` is already set (`setEnvDefaults`).
2. **Otherwise, request headers** — `x-forwarded-host` (falling back to `host`) plus `x-forwarded-proto` (falling back to the framework protocol, then `https`).

There's a `trustHost` gate around this too: `setEnvDefaults` sets `trustHost` true if `AUTH_URL`/`AUTH_TRUST_HOST`/`VERCEL`/`CF_PAGES` is set or `NODE_ENV !== "production"`; otherwise core throws `UntrustedHost`. Note `AUTH_URL` being set *also* implicitly enables `trustHost`.

In the Next.js integration there's an extra step: `reqWithEnvURL()` (`packages/next-auth/src/lib/env.ts:7`) rewrites the incoming request's origin to the env URL's origin *before* core ever sees it, so every downstream consumer (including the OAuth `redirect_uri` and callback URL) sees the pinned origin.

## Why pinning `AUTH_URL` fixed your case

Your ingress strips `X-Forwarded-Host` / `X-Forwarded-Proto`. On the header branch, `x-forwarded-host` is absent, so it falls through to `host` — the pod's internal address — and `x-forwarded-proto` falls through too, yielding internal `http://…` callback URLs. Setting `AUTH_URL=https://app.acme.dev` takes branch 1 and short-circuits header detection completely, so the internal host is never consulted. That's the intended escape hatch for exactly this situation (and why the docs now call `AUTH_URL` "mostly unnecessary with v5" but still the correct lever when headers can't be trusted).

One caveat to keep in mind: with `AUTH_URL=https://app.acme.dev` (pathname `/`), `basePath` stays whatever the framework default is (`/auth` for core, `/api/auth` for `next-auth`), and it simply appends it — so your callback is `https://app.acme.dev/api/auth/callback/<provider>`. Make sure that exact URL is registered with each provider.

Understood — no header changes, no platform ticket. `AUTH_URL=https://app.acme.dev` is the right and complete fix on your side; header trust is off the table and the code path already honors that.

Two small things worth a glance later, purely config-side, no infra involved:

- Provider registries: each OAuth provider must have `https://app.acme.dev/api/auth/callback/<provider>` registered exactly, since that's what gets emitted.
- Client-side/Middleware: `next-auth/react` uses `NEXTAUTH_URL`/`VERCEL_URL` at build time (`packages/next-auth/src/react.tsx`), so if any client code constructs auth URLs, make sure `AUTH_URL` (or `NEXTAUTH_URL`) is present in the build/runtime env too, not just the server.
